name: Macadamia oil

card.summary: A palmitoleic- and oleic-rich nut oil used as a cosmetic emollient and cooking oil, with composition research but no clear human skin-appearance trials.
card.note: Nut allergy is a consideration for any macadamia-derived product.

quick.overview:
Macadamia oil is pressed from the kernels of Macadamia integrifolia and related trees native to eastern Australia. It is mostly monounsaturated, with oleic acid and an unusual amount of palmitoleic acid, and it is used both in cooking and as an emollient in skin and hair products.

Research in the sources covers its fatty acids, oxidative stability and effects of dietary palmitoleic acid on blood lipids. No published human trial was found testing it on skin appearance.
quick.mechanism: As a topical ingredient it works as an emollient and fragrance fixative. Its low polyunsaturated content is linked to good oxidative stability. Palmitoleic acid has been studied in diet and metabolism research, not in skin-care trials.
quick.risks: Sources do not describe specific topical safety data. As a tree-nut product it can matter to people with nut allergy, a general consideration rather than a finding in the supplied studies.

lead: Macadamia oil is a non-volatile oil pressed from the kernels of the macadamia tree, chiefly Macadamia integrifolia, a species native to Australia and now grown commercially [1]. It is mostly monounsaturated: oleic acid is the main fatty acid, and palmitoleic acid, unusual in plant oils, is also present in notable amounts [1]. People who use it on skin and hair value it for the soft, conditioned feel an emollient oil leaves, and it appears as an ingredient in moisturizers, hair care and massage products.

It is used as a frying and salad oil and in cosmetics, where it serves as an emollient and fragrance fixative [1]. Research involving the oil covers composition across cultivars, oxidative stability and, in animals, lipid-lowering and antioxidant effects; studies of palmitoleic acid look at blood lipids and metabolism rather than skin [3][4][5][11]. No clinical study of its effect on human skin or hair appearance was found.
infobox: Clear, light amber, slightly nutty odour[1]

paras: Reference sources give oleic acid as the dominant fatty acid, with palmitoleic acid at roughly a fifth of the oil by one estimate, linoleic acid around 1 to 3 percent and alpha-linolenic acid 1 to 2 percent; exact ranges differ between sources.[1][2] A comparison of oils from 15 cultivars grown in China found differences in composition and antioxidant capacity.[3] Studies on the oxidative stability of culinary oils include macadamia among the oils examined.[5] The low polyunsaturated content is linked to the oil's stability.[1]

The kernel is about two-thirds to three-quarters oil, which accumulates after the nut reaches full size and the shell hardens [1]. Trees raised from seed bear in roughly five to seven years, and commercial orchards use grafted plants [1][12]. Wikipedia reports that South Africa has been the largest macadamia producer since the 2010s, having overtaken Australia and Hawaii, with about 87,000 tonnes in 2024 [12]. The oil is clear to light amber with a faintly nutty smell, and the oil's high stability is attributed to its low polyunsaturated content [1].

In cosmetics the oil is used as an emollient and fragrance fixative.[1] As a food it is used for frying and, more often unheated, in dressings.[1] A Grokipedia entry attributes moisture-retention and wrinkle-reduction figures to cosmetic formulations containing the oil; that claim comes from an AI-generated source and was not matched to a trial in the supplied literature.[2]

Cosmetic formularies use macadamia oil as an emollient, meaning an ingredient that softens skin by filling gaps between surface cells and reducing water loss, and as a fragrance fixative that helps scent last [1]. Its fatty-acid profile, rich in oleic and palmitoleic acids, is the basis for its use in products aimed at dry skin and hair conditioning. Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, credits macadamia-containing formulations with improved moisture retention and wrinkle reduction, but that account did not point to a published trial and its figures are unverified [2].

No published trial was located that tested macadamia oil on skin hydration, hair shine or wrinkles. The nearest registered studies are an eczema moisturizer evaluation and a skincare product study that do not isolate the oil [13][14].

Recent studies in mice report that macadamia oil reduced body weight, serum cholesterol and triglycerides in high-fat-diet animals and improved liver enzyme levels, with activation of the AMPK and antioxidant Nrf2 pathways proposed as the mechanism [11][15]. Other mouse work reported protective effects against chemically induced colitis and against brain injury from a toxic metal compound [16][17]. A study of the press cake in hyperlipidemic rats looked at blood lipids and gut microbiota [18]. These results concern ingestion in animals, and they have not been replicated as topical benefits.

Because macadamia oil is a source of palmitoleic acid, studies of that fatty acid are sometimes associated with it. A controlled diet study in hypercholesterolemic men compared palmitoleic, palmitic and oleic acids on plasma lipids,[6] and animal studies examined its effects on lipoproteins in hamsters and on metabolic syndrome in rats.[7][8] A review discussed palmitoleate and glucose homeostasis.[4] These concern dietary intake, not topical use.

Macadamia is a tree nut. Wikipedia reports that macadamia allergy is relatively uncommon among people with tree-nut allergy but can range up to anaphylaxis and can cross-react with coconut, walnut, hazelnut and cashew [12]. The same page notes that macadamia nuts are toxic to dogs, causing weakness and hind-limb paralysis, and to cats [12].

The macadamia tree is native to the rainforests of eastern Australia. Allan Cunningham was the first European to encounter it, in 1828, and the genus was named in 1857 by Ferdinand von Mueller after the chemist and medical teacher John Macadam [12]. Aboriginal peoples had long used the nut as a bushfood [12]. William Purvis brought seed to Hawaii in the early 1880s, planting it at Kapulena as a windbreak for sugarcane, and Hawaii became the world's largest producer for more than a century [12]. Grokipedia adds that Indigenous Australians also used the oil as a liniment, a detail from a single AI-generated source [2]. The first commercial orchard was planted near Lismore, New South Wales, in the late 1880s [12].

No studies found on macadamia oil applied to skin or hair. Registered trials only loosely related to the oil include a study of dietary macronutrients on digestive and cardiovascular health (n=24) [9] and a trial of a vegetable-oil nutritional supplement in people at risk of diabetes (n=25) [10]; neither tests topical or cosmetic use.

Related human research concerns palmitoleic acid, a fatty acid in the oil. A controlled diet study in hypercholesterolemic men compared palmitoleic, palmitic and oleic acids on plasma lipids [6], and a review discussed palmitoleate and glucose homeostasis [4]. Animal studies of macadamia oil itself are described above.

chain: Lipid-rich oil spreads over skin or hair
Emollient film softens and conditions the surface
angle.text: Macadamia oil is used as an emollient in creams, lotions and hair products, and some people apply it directly to skin or hair for softness and shine. The effect described is surface conditioning, and no trial of the oil on skin or hair appearance was located.
